title: A Birefringence-Blind Consistency Test of the Planck Cosmic Birefringence Hint
speaker: Anto I. Lonappan (UCSD)
abstract:
Abstract:
Several analyses of Planck, ACT, and WMAP data report a small uniform rotation of CMB polarization, β ≈ 0.3–0.4°. If real, this would be evidence of parity-violating physics such as axion-like fields coupled to photons. At this level, however, the signal is exactly degenerate with an overall miscalibration of the detectors' polarization angles. The leading method, the Minami–Komatsu (MK) likelihood, breaks this degeneracy by using Galactic dust as a calibrator. That makes its detector angles, and therefore β, dependent on how the dust EB correlation is modeled.

In this talk, I will present a complementary test that never uses that foreground model. For any pair of maps, the cosmic rotation cancels exactly, leaving only the relative instrumental angle. We measure these relative angles from antisymmetric and symmetric cross-spectra. We then combine all pairs into a gauge-fixed calibration network, with maps as nodes and pairwise angles as edges, to reconstruct each detector's calibration offset.

Applied to eight Planck NPIPE detector-set maps, the network reconstruction agrees with the MK calibration pattern (χ² = 8.18 for 7 degrees of freedom, PTE = 0.32), with no map deviating by more than 1.8σ. I will explain what this does and does not tell us. Because both methods use the same maps, this is an independent method rather than independent data. It supports the calibration foundation of the β hint but cannot fix its absolute zero point.

I will close by discussing how a sub-0.1° external calibration anchor, combined with this network, could deliver an absolute birefringence measurement. This will be possible with BICEP/Keck, SPT-3G, the Simons Observatory, and LiteBIRD.

About the Astro/Cosmology Seminar series:
The Center for Dark Cosmology and Gravitation seminar series (aka, the Department of Physics Astrophysics and Cosmology Seminar) will showcase key developments in astrophysics and cosmology, the implications of these for fundamental physics, and vice versa, the implications of laboratory particle physics discoveries for our understanding of the cosmos. Among the outstanding issues in physics, the nature of the dark matter and dark energy and the origin of the supermassive black holes very early in the history of the universe stand out as venues where beyond standard model physics is at play or likely plays a role. The pace of discovery in this field is breathtaking. The advent of gravitational wave observatories, the James Webb Space Telescope, and the Simons Observatory for the cosmic microwave background all complement a host of laboratory experiments including LHC, short and long baseline neutrino oscillation experiments, neutrino less double beta decay searches, and direct dark matter detection experiments, to name just a few. Moreover, all of these research thrusts are underpinned by rapid development of computational capabilities and artificial intelligence. The CDCG is dedicated to facilitating and bridging laboratory, observational, theoretical and computational studies focussed on the cosmos.

title: Tuning Quantum Materials with Extreme Pressure and Magnetic Field
speaker: Yuhang Deng (Dept. of Physics, UCSD)
abstract:
Abstract: Correlated electron materials based on lanthanides, actinides, and transition metals host a rich landscape of emergent phenomena, including unconventional superconductivity, exotic magnetism, heavy-fermion behavior, and nontrivial topological states. These phenomena emerge from the interplay among strong electronic correlations, spin–orbit coupling, and competing energy scales, and can be dramatically modified by external parameters such as pressure, magnetic field, and chemical composition.

In this talk, I will discuss our efforts to uncover and control quantum phases in correlated materials under extreme conditions of high pressure and high magnetic fields. Using diamond anvil cells, which enable electrical, magnetic, and optical measurements at high pressures, together with complementary high-field techniques, we investigate how these tuning parameters
reshape electronic, magnetic, and structural properties. I will highlight three examples: pressure-induced metallization and suppression of a magnetically ordered conducting surface state in FeSi; pressure-driven structural and valence evolution, and new superconductivity in UTe 2 ; and the emergence and evolution of multiple superconducting states in U 1-x Th x Te 2 under high magnetic fields. Together, these studies demonstrate how pressure, magnetic field, and chemical substitution can tune the delicate balance among competing interactions in correlated electron systems, providing new perspectives on the mechanisms underlying unconventional superconductivity, magnetism, and topological quantum states.

Yuhang Deng received his Ph.D. in Physics from Washington University in St. Louis in 2019. He subsequently joined Prof. M. Brian Maple’s group at the University of California San Diego, where he worked as a postdoctoral scholar and is currently an Assistant Project Scientist. His research focuses on the experimental study of quantum materials under extreme conditions, particularly superconductivity and magnetism at high pressures and high magnetic fields. His broader research interests include topological and Kondo insulators, unconventional superconductors, and the application of diamond nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers to high-pressure physics.

title: Modeling density variations in microtubule-based two-dimensional active nematics
speaker: Kevin  Mitchell (UC Merced)
abstract: Abstract: A dense two-dimensional layer of aligned microtubules (MTs), powered by molecular motors, is a canonical laboratory model of active materials and a synthetic analog of biological systems such as bacterial turbulence, mitotic spindles, and morphogenesis. This material exhibits nematic ordering and associated topological defects, which display complex emergent dynamics, including the creation and annihilation of defects and the braiding of defects around one another in a complicated chaotic dance. Despite its prominent role in research, the MT-based active nematic material lacks a well established theoretical model that accurately captures the rich density variations prominently seen in experiments—--density variations that are, in fact, the experimental signature of the nematic structure itself. The MT-system is typically modeled using two fields: the Q-tensor (encoding the order and orientation of the nematic phase) and the fluid velocity; critically, the microtubule density is assumed to be constant. This traditional model is adopted from classical Landau-de Gennes liquid crystal theory. In this talk, we present a fundamentally different approach to modeling MT-based active nematics that explicitly incorporates density variations, producing simulations that strongly resemble experimental videos, including the characteristic striation patterns. It also reproduces important behavior of the system confined to a circular well—behavior seen experimentally, but not captured by current theory. In crafting our model, we present an alternative to Landau-de Gennes theory for the creation and annihilation of topological defects that does not rely on the classic isotropic-nematic phase transition.

title: Superconductivity and magnetism in crystalline graphite allotropes
speaker: Andrea Young (UC Santa Barbara)
abstract: I will describe the physics of graphite crystals with rhombohedral stacking, where the competition between electron hopping within- and between- the graphene planes leads to a flat electronic dispersion and the crystallinity leads to a near total absence of disorder. The high electronic density of states and Berry curvature—-both of which can be tuned by a perpendicular electric field—lead to a dizzying variety of magnetic and superconducting states, often within the same device, while the high experimental reproducibility enabled by the crystalline nature of these structurally simple systems allows us to investigate a variety of correlated electron phenomena. I will focus on our efforts to use scanning nanoscale magnetometry to probe the nature and origins of magnetism and unconventional superconductivity, as well as the fate of the correlated electron liquid at high temperatures.
